name: Goldberger Textile Collection
description: On Lajos utca in Óbuda, the Goldberger Textile Collection occupies the former main building of the Goldberger company, a textile printing firm whose roots go back to the 1780s. The permanent exhibition follows the family and the factory from the 1784 blue-dyeing workshop to the winding-up of the factory, with interactive elements that explain textile printing.

children.text: The Goldberger Textile Collection is part of the Óbuda Museum's network, at Lajos utca 138 in Óbuda. It occupies the former main building of the Goldberger company, which the museum's own profile says was founded in 1784. The building is over 200 years old according to the museum's profile, and the museum says the family's first workshop opened in the present building at the end of the 18th century.

Sources disagree slightly on the start of the firm. The museum gives 1784, while Wikipedia says that Ferenc Goldberg founded a dyeing factory on today's Lajos utca in 1785 with a Czech bluemaker named Stibrall. The firm modernised under later generations. Wikipedia records a perrotine printing machine bought in 1845, a visit by Emperor Franz Joseph I in 1857 and the family's ennoblement with the prefix Buday in 1867.

Leó Goldberger became chairman and chief executive in 1920, and the company set up a weaving mill in Kelenföld in 1923 and a spinning mill in 1927. It reached its peak in 1938-1939. Leó Goldberger was arrested by the Gestapo on 19 March 1944 and died at Mauthausen concentration camp on 5 May 1945. The factory was nationalised in 1948, later became part of BUDAPRINT, which went bankrupt in 1989, when liquidation proceedings were opened against it.

According to the museum's own site, the permanent exhibition has five units. They follow the Goldberger family from its settlement in Óbuda and the founding of the blue-dyeing workshop in 1784, through the growth into a factory, mechanisation and international success under Leó Goldberger, to the years under the planned economy and the winding-up of the factory, and the display uses interactive elements to explain textile printing. Older listings mention a display about a Tamási slipper workshop, but the museum's current exhibition page does not, and a 2014 Infostart report says the workshop's machines were shown in Óbuda until 2012 and then went back to Tamási.
Sewing machines, scale models and authentic copies of equipment give a physical idea of how patterned cloth was produced.
Good to know
Check the official Óbuda Museum site for current opening times and tickets for the Textile Museum.
The collection is at Lajos utca 138, away from Fő tér; check the route before you go.
According to the museum's visitor page, the nearest stops are Tímár utca and Szentlélek tér on the H5 suburban railway, and the museum has no public parking.

The Goldberger permanent exhibition (museum.hu)

historyIntro: The Goldberger Textile Collection recalls Óbuda's industrial era through one of Hungary's historically important textile enterprises.

historySections.heading: A factory woven into the district

children.text: The Goldberger company became a well-known name in Hungarian textile manufacturing. The museum collection stands in the former factory premises on Lajos Street, connecting industrial history with the architecture of the workplace.

historySections.heading: Fabric as a record of social change

children.text: Textile production reveals changing tastes, technology, labour and everyday consumption. The Óbuda Museum collection preserves those stories through manufacturing objects and examples of the fabrics associated with the enterprise.

name: Aquincum Museum
description: The Aquincum Museum and its archaeological park in Óbuda preserve part of the Roman civil town of Aquincum. A neoclassical museum building opened in 1894, ruins of streets, houses and a Mithras temple stand outdoors, and the best-known find is a Roman water organ dated to AD 228.

children.text: The Aquincum Museum is in the Óbuda district, on the site of the Roman town of Aquincum. Aquincum began as a military base on the frontier of the Roman Empire, and Legio II Adiutrix was stationed there by AD 89. After Pannonia was reorganised in AD 103 it became capital of Pannonia Inferior, and it later received municipal status and then the rank of colonia. By the end of the 2nd century the town had at least 30,000 inhabitants according to Wikipedia.

Roman remains first came to light in 1778, when a vine-grower found part of an underfloor heating system. One source says Maria Theresa ordered the baths left open under protective cover, making them Hungary's first protected historic monument. Professional excavations began in the later 19th century, and the museum's neoclassical exhibition building opened on 10 May 1894.

Outdoors, the archaeological park contains part of the civil town. Visitors see excavated houses, shops and a market along two streets, a civilian amphitheatre, a reconstructed Roman house known as the House of the Painter and a reconstructed Mithras temple. Indoors, the collections include finds from the local mithraeum and a very large body of archaeological material. Wikipedia says the Budapest History Museum, to which Aquincum belongs, holds more than a million objects.

The best-known object is the Aquincum water organ. Remains were found in 1931 when the archaeologist Lajos Nagy excavated the civil town's fire brigade building, and bronze plates indicate that the instrument was given to the fire brigade in AD 228. Wikipedia calls it the only Roman water organ known to survive. In 2007 a former transformer house on the grounds became the museum's new main building, with the exhibition Rome in Aquincum, which displays the organ.

The Second World War did serious damage. Bombing of the nearby Óbuda gas factory damaged the museum building by about 40 percent, the ruin area was hit by twelve bombs and almost half the finds were destroyed. The permanent exhibition reopened in 1948. The wider Budapest History Museum network also includes Roman sites in Óbuda such as a Baths Museum and a Military Town Museum.
Good to know
Check the official Aquincum Museum and Budapest History Museum sites for current opening times, tickets and which exhibitions are running.
The outdoor archaeological park is a large site, so allow time for a walk between the museum and the ruins; wear comfortable shoes.
The Baths Museum and Military Town Museum are separate Roman sites in Óbuda; check the official sites for how to visit them.

heroImage.alt: The columned Aquincum Museum building behind Roman ruins

historyIntro: Aquincum is where Budapest's Roman history becomes tangible, through the surviving streets, baths and public spaces of an ancient settlement.

children.text: Aquincum developed as an important Roman centre in the region of present-day Óbuda. Its archaeological remains include residential buildings, spaces for trade and bathing, and traces of the public life of a provincial settlement.
The museum's ruin garden brings visitors close to the surviving walls of the civilian town. Exhibited finds help interpret how Romans lived, worked, gathered and adopted customs far from Rome itself.

stories.title: Why some call Aquincum the Hungarian Pompeii

children.text: Travel guides such as We Love Budapest describe the open-air archaeological site as 'the Hungarian Pompeii', a nickname rather than an official title. The comparison is a modern description of the extensive ruins, not a claim that Aquincum was buried by the eruption at Vesuvius.

name: Budapest History Museum — Castle Museum
description: The Castle Museum occupies Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, and tells the story of Budapest from prehistory to the late twentieth century. Its most distinctive rooms are the restored medieval palace spaces in the basement and a hall of Gothic sculpture found buried in 1974.

children.text: The Castle Museum is the part of the Budapest History Museum housed in Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, with its main entrance from the Lion Courtyard. Its displays cover roughly two thousand years of the city's past, arranged from the medieval palace in the basement up to prehistory on the top floor.

The basement is the reason many people come. After the damage of the Second World War, archaeologists uncovered the remains of the medieval royal palace beneath the later buildings. The Gothic Hall, built by King Sigismund in the early fifteenth century, is an irregular rectangle of 20.2 by 11.55 metres divided into two naves with rib vaults. Its ribs, pillars, arches and window niches were restored by the sculptor Ernő Szakál in 1961 and 1962, and the architect László Gerő planned the wider reconstruction. Nearby are the palace chapel, stretches of castle wall and a room devoted to the Corvina library.

On the ground floor are the Gothic sculptures from the royal palace. In 1974 a sealed cellar of a townhouse in front of the palace yielded more than sixty sculptural torsos and thousands of fragments from the court of King Sigismund of Luxembourg, who reigned from 1387 to 1437. Some pieces still carry traces of paint, and many were never finished; one guide says the workshop broke up before the work was done, though the reasons remain unclear.

Upstairs, Budapest, Light and Shadow follows about a thousand years of the city's history, while a second exhibition follows the Royal Palace itself from 1686 to today. The top floor, In Pursuit of Lost Times, begins with stone tools about fifty thousand years old and runs to the Hungarian conquest.

The museum has older roots than the castle. Budapest's city assembly decided to found a municipal museum in 1887, and the medieval department and the directorate moved into the restored castle in 1967, after which the whole institution became known as the Budapest History Museum. It also runs the Kiscelli Museum, the Budapest Gallery and the Medieval Jewish Prayer House.
Good to know
The entrance is in the Lion Courtyard of Building E on the Buda Castle hill; a second entrance leads to the King's Cellar. Check the official site for current opening times and tickets.
The Hungarian National Gallery and the National Széchényi Library are in the same palace complex, so the museum fits easily into a longer castle visit.
One visitor guide notes that the basement level with the medieval rooms cannot be reached by wheelchair; confirm access arrangements on the official page.

historyIntro: The Castle Museum uses the layers of Buda's Royal Palace to tell the story of the city from antiquity to the modern era.

children.text: The museum is housed inside Buda Castle, itself a structure transformed by medieval royal life, Ottoman-era conflict and later rebuilding. Rooms and surviving fragments link physical architecture to the city's changing political role.

historySections.heading: From separate towns to a capital

children.text: The permanent exhibitions explore Roman Aquincum, the medieval royal palace, the Ottoman wars, the fusion of Buda, Pest and Óbuda and the city's rapid growth around 1900. Visitors can see how the modern metropolis emerged from communities with distinct histories.

name: Kiscelli Museum
description: Set in a Baroque Trinitarian monastery on a plateau above Óbuda, the Kiscelli Museum shows Budapest's urban history from the eighteenth century on and houses the Budapest Municipal Gallery. Its bare-brick former church, now an exhibition and concert space, is the building's most unusual interior.

children.text: The Kiscelli Museum stands at Kiscelli utca 108 in Óbuda, on a plateau above Bécsi út, and is a branch of the Budapest History Museum. It presents the history of Budapest from the eighteenth century onward and is also the home of the Budapest Municipal Gallery, the Fővárosi Képtár.

The building began as a Trinitarian monastery. The Baroque complex was built from 1745 to 1758 to designs by the Viennese architect Johann Entzenhoffer, with a church beside the north wing of the two-storey friary. A copy of the Mariazell cult statue was placed there, and the site became a place of pilgrimage known as Kiscell, from the German Klein Zell. One visitor guide gives 1760 as the year the church was consecrated.

In the 1780s, under Joseph II, the order was dissolved; sources give 1783 or 1784. It served as a military hospital, barracks and storage space. Around 1911 (sources give 1910 or 1911) the Viennese furniture manufacturer and collector Miksa Schmidt bought the property and converted it into a mansion, and for a long time it was called the Schmidt Castle. When he died, his will of 1935 left the complex to the capital city for use as a museum.

The Second World War did great damage, and the fighting of November 1956 caused more. A visitor guide reports that the roof was destroyed and that a new one was built between 1976 and 1983, with the church interior deliberately left as bare brick. The former church, with its raw brick nave and empty niches, now hosts large temporary exhibitions and concerts, and the Municipal Gallery held its first exhibition in the ruin in 1988.

The permanent rooms hold some distinctive objects: the original 1712 figures from the Holy Trinity column that stands in front of Matthias Church, a collection of old Pest and Buda shop signs, the complete fittings of the Golden Lion pharmacy and a printing room with a Columbia press. Around the museum lies the Kiscelli park forest, about fifteen hectares of woodland that Schmidt laid out as the mansion's grounds.
Good to know
A visitor guide lists tram 17 from Széll Kálmán tér, or trams 19 and 41 from Batthyány tér to Szent Margit Kórház, then a steep walk up Kiscelli utca. Bus 165 from Kolosy tér avoids the climb.
One visitor guide says there is no lift and the upper floor cannot be reached by wheelchair, and that some permanent-room labels are in Hungarian only. Check the official site for access details.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the programme of exhibitions and concerts in the church space.
Allow time for a walk in the Kiscelli park forest around the museum.

historyIntro: Kiscelli Museum occupies an evocative historic complex in Óbuda, where the history of the building adds another layer to its collections.

children.text: The complex's past includes religious use, later military and residential functions and wartime shelter. Its architecture preserves traces of the changing roles that historic buildings can acquire across centuries.

historySections.heading: A home for urban history and art

children.text: As part of the Budapest History Museum, Kiscelli holds collections about the modern city's social and material culture alongside fine art. The museum grounds connect indoor exhibits to the building's complicated past.
